doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Teaching jazz by ear: singing a Parker tune on the snare
summary: He explains his aural teaching method, having students vocalize 'Billie's Bounce' and then translate it to drums.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You must be reading my notes here because I had a question about that and what methods you might have used to lay the groundwork to increase the chances that a student could be successful in improvising and have a creative spirit?
Okay, well for me the defining factor is how well one listens and perceives sound. And there is a very corny adage which is very true is if you can’t say it you can’t play it. So

my teaching over the years became less and less visual, meaning exercises out of a book, and more and more aural. And what I found was that another impediment to one’s learning ability was the ability to internalize the music and especially as a jazz player. Because you know when a drummer is playing the tune and when the drummer is just playing his licks. When you listen to somebody like Roy Haynes and hear how he orchestrates the tune, I mean it’s right there. Billy Higgins, Philly Joe, all the great drummers up to Brian Blade today and on. They’re playing the music. They’re not playing the drums. So my thrust with the student now is to get them to be able to vocalize, say just as an example, a Charlie Parker tune. Something simple like “Billie’s Bounce.” And when they first sing it they go [scats] right? So they baby talk it. So I say okay find a recording of it, listen to Mr. Parker and the other horns, and get to the point where you can vocalize a reasonable facsimile of the horn. Because as a drummer you have to be an inner horn player. Because those are the people whom you accompany. And just like I tell horn players. You need to learn something about drums and how to listen to drums, because those are the people you’re playing with. So at any rate, yeah, so I get them to vocalize. And if they can internalize that, some people can, some people cannot. Some people do it easily, some people give up very quickly. And it’s like learning a language obviously. And once they’ve got that I say okay, let’s go to the drums. Now you be Charlie Parker only instead of playing an alto saxophone you’re playing a snare drum. Let me hear you play the snare drum with the same flow as Mr. Parker gets with air. I want to hear you get it with motion. See if you can translate [scats] not into [scats] but [scats] right? And they struggle, just as anybody does with something new, but that’s where it all comes from is the struggle. You say, “Okay — it doesn’t sound like Bird, does it. “No man, it doesn’t at all.” I say, “Are you uptight? Are you tense?” “Oh yeah. I’m trying as hard as I can.” Well quit trying. Quit trying. Just let the sticks dance on the drums and then you might make some remarks like, “Hey, look at your hand. Look how tightly it’s holding the stick. Just hold the stick so that, like if you were picking up something that was very fragile. Don’t squeeze it, just let it rest in your hand. Same way if you were an artist you would use a paint brush.” Boom, all these different avenues of connections that you try to make. And lo and behold there it comes. And once you’ve got the melody and you can play it on the snare, then you say okay, let’s add some accompaniment to it. Let’s put a ride cymbal here, and let’s put a hi-hat on two and four, and let’s outline the melody between the snare drum and the bass drum. And all of a sudden they go, “Wow man, I sound like Philly Joe.” And you say, “Well almost.” But the point is using music as the model — using an auditory model not a visual one.
